scenarioName: Syncope on Warfarin — Occult GI Hemorrhage and the High-Risk Refusal

scenarioStory.history: 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on warfarin who lost consciousness while standing for a hymn during the 10:00 service. Witnesses say she went pale, her knees buckled, and she went down into the pew — she was out for perhaps 15 to 20 seconds, with no shaking, no incontinence, and no confusion afterward. She struck her right shoulder on the pew arm on the way down but did not hit her head. She is now awake, fully oriented, embarrassed by the attention, and adamant that she just stood up too fast. What she does not volunteer, and what only emerges on direct questioning, is that she has had a dull, gnawing epigastric ache for two days, has felt 'wrung out and weak' since yesterday, and passed a black, tarry, foul-smelling stool this morning that she dismissed as 'my iron pills, or something I ate.' She has not taken iron in years. She has been taking ibuprofen two or three times a day for the past week and a half for a sore shoulder — on top of warfarin. She lives alone. Her husband died four years ago and her daughter is two hours away in Milwaukee.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: This is the most dangerous patient a crew will meet all shift, and she is going to smile at them and ask them to leave. She is A&O×4, her vitals look unremarkable, and she has a perfectly plausible story — she stood up too fast during a hymn. Every instinct says vasovagal, sign the refusal, clear the call. Here is what MATC actually says. The Syncope guideline's Review of Systems has a line item for OCCULT BLOOD LOSS (GI/GU), and its list of high-risk causes of syncope names GI BLEED explicitly under hemorrhagic. Its Additional Evaluation is not optional: cardiac monitoring, SpO2, ongoing vitals, 12-lead EKG, and a blood glucose. And its Key Consideration 2 is the sentence that governs this whole call — decisions about delayed or non-transport are for patients where a LOWER-RISK etiology is suspected, and they are made in consultation with medical direction. Nothing about a 72-year-old anticoagulated woman who syncopes is low-risk. The crew's job in this phase is to do the workup the protocol demands and to ask the questions that make her stop being reassuring — because she will not offer the melena. Someone has to ask. → Melena revealed; she still refuses: The crew asked, and the picture inverts. Two days of gnawing epigastric pain. Profound weakness since yesterday. A black, tarry, foul-smelling stool this morning that she rationalized as iron pills she does not take. And ten days of daily ibuprofen layered on top of warfarin — an NSAID stripping her gastric mucosa while an anticoagulant guarantees that whatever it opens will not close. This is an upper GI hemorrhage in a fully anticoagulated 72-year-old, and MATC's Abdominal Pain guideline flags it in one sentence: abdominal pain in older adults, patients with bleeding disorders, and patients on anticoagulation medications may be a harbinger for severe illness. Her repeat pressure has slipped and her pulse has climbed as far as a beta-blocked heart can take it. AND SHE STILL SAYS NO. She is competent, she understands the words, and she is still going to walk to her car. This is where the protocol stops being about medicine and becomes about disposition: MATC's Syncope guideline authorizes delayed or non-transport ONLY where a LOWER-RISK etiology is suspected, and ONLY in consultation with medical direction. GI bleed is on the protocol's high-risk list by name. The crew cannot make this decision alone, and the protocol never asked them to. → Med control consulted; transport accepted: The physician on the radio said the words the crew could not make land: you are bleeding internally, your blood thinner means it will not stop on its own, and if you go home you may not wake up. She agreed to go. She is on the monitor in atrial fibrillation, has two lines, and is receiving fluid titrated to a MAP of 65 while the crew watches her EtCO2 as a perfusion tracer. Note what actually saved this patient — not a drug, not a procedure. Someone asked about her stool. Someone did a 12-lead she said she did not need. Someone called a physician instead of accepting a signature. MATC's Syncope guideline says EMS clinicians, by being most proximate to the scene and the presentation, are commonly in a unique position to identify the cause of syncope. That is exactly what happened here, and it happened because the crew treated a well-appearing woman as a hemorrhage patient on the strength of one question.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Fainted during the hymn at church and went down in the pew. She is awake now, insists she is fine, and wants to go home.

relatedChecklist: ASK about occult blood loss (GI/GU) directly and in private — she will not volunteer the melena
Do the required syncope workup: cardiac monitor, SpO2, 12-lead EKG, BGL, ongoing vitals
Evaluate for hemorrhage and treat for shock if indicated; establish IV access
Recognize compensated shock behind 'normal' vitals — she is beta-blocked and cannot mount a tachycardia
Screen the fall for trauma — geriatric patients falling from standing sustain significant injury
Move her out of the crowded foyer — you will not get a stool history with 15 neighbors listening

relatedChecklist: Name the risk: anticoagulated older adult with abdominal pain = harbinger of severe illness
GI bleed is a named HIGH-RISK cause of syncope — this is not vasovagal
Contact online medical direction — non-transport requires consultation, and this is NOT low-risk
IV access (2 attempts or 90 sec → IO); fluid bolus titrated to MAP 65; EtCO2 <25 = poor perfusion
Serial vitals q5 min and DOCUMENT the trend — the trend is the argument
Advance notification: anticoagulated GI bleed with syncope — they will need reversal and endoscopy

relatedChecklist: Titrate isotonic fluid to MAP 65 — boluses pressure-infused over <15 min, reassess after each
Keep her on the monitor — recurrent arrhythmia is a live risk in syncope
Watch for decompensation — falling EtCO2, rising cap refill, mentation change
Handoff: syncope + melena + warfarin + NSAIDs + trend — give them the reasoning, not just numbers

scenarioEvents.name: Refusal accepted; no workup, no med control
scenarioEvents.description: The crew took the easy story. No 12-lead, no monitor, no question about her stool, no call to medical direction — just a signature on a refusal form and a well-appearing 72-year-old walking out to her car. She made it about forty feet across the parking lot before her second syncopal episode, and this time there was no pew to catch her. She struck the back of her head on the asphalt. She is now a fully anticoagulated patient with a head injury and an ongoing GI hemorrhage, which is roughly the worst combination in geriatric prehospital medicine: warfarin means an intracranial bleed does not tamponade, and the GI bleed means she has no reserve to lose. She is GCS 12 and dropping, hypotensive at 82/48, with a boggy occipital hematoma. Everything the crew skipped is now mandatory, and it is being done in a parking lot with a worse patient. Note the honest part of this failure: she had capacity. She could have refused even a perfect crew. But a perfect crew would have done the workup, found the melena, called a physician, and documented all of it — and the protocol says that is what non-transport requires.
relatedChecklist: Maintain SBP ≥110 — give fluid to PREVENT hypotension, do not wait until she is already hypotensive
High-flow O2 via NRB as a precaution against unanticipated deterioration
Do NOT hyperventilate — maintain EtCO2 35–45; hypocapnia worsens secondary brain injury
Assume c-spine injury — moderate head injury with altered mental status; collar her
Preferential transport to the highest level of trauma care — GCS 3–13 meets the criterion
Trend GCS and pupils — recheck pupils with ANY decrease in mentation
Do not forget the GI bleed — she is hemorrhaging from two places now; fluid targets BOTH
